nameStory: Mat sandbur gets its name from two key features: it grows in a low, spreading 'mat' pattern across sandy soils, and its seeds form spiny 'burs' that stick to everything they touch. The word 'bur' comes from the same root as 'burrow' - these seeds literally burrow into fur, fabric, and skin with their sharp, backward-pointing spines.
description: Mat sandbur is a sprawling summer grass that forms low mats across sandy ground, rarely growing more than a foot tall. This native grass produces clusters of spiny seed heads that look deceptively innocent until you brush against them. The seeds are enclosed in hard, round burs covered with needle-sharp spines that grab onto anything that passes by. It's a tough, drought-tolerant grass that thrives in poor, sandy soils where other plants struggle.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round, hard burs about the size of a small pea, covered in sharp spines that feel like tiny needles and stick painfully to skin and clothing

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, with stems that branch out sideways rather than growing tall and upright

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow grass blades that feel rough to the touch and may have small hairs along the edges

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Inconspicuous grass flowers that quickly develop into the characteristic spiny seed clusters

habitat: Mat sandbur thrives in sandy, well-drained soils where few other plants can compete - think beaches, sandy roadsides, vacant lots, and disturbed ground. In New England, it's most commonly found along the coast and in sandy inland areas. It particularly loves sunny, open spaces with poor soil that stays relatively dry.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small tufts of narrow grass leaves, growing low and spreading outward rather than upward.
seasonality.summer: Plants flower and quickly develop their notorious spiny seed burs, which become increasingly problematic as the season progresses.
seasonality.fall: Mature burs are at their stickiest and most painful, readily attaching to passing animals, people, and clothing for seed dispersal.
seasonality.winter: This annual grass dies back, but dried burs may persist on the ground, still capable of sticking to unwary passersby.

funFact: Mat sandbur burs are so effective at hitching rides that they've inspired the design of Velcro - the spines have backward-pointing barbs that make them nearly impossible to remove without carefully working them out spine by spine.
confusionNotes: Other bur-producing plants like burdock have much larger, softer burs that feel prickly but not needle-sharp, and grow on tall, broad-leaved plants rather than low grass mats. Remember: if it's a low grass with tiny, rock-hard burs that feel like stepping on thumbtacks, it's sandbur.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its painful reputation, mat sandbur is actually a native New England plant that's been here long before human settlement. It's often mistakenly considered a 'weed' because it thrives in disturbed areas, but it's actually an important pioneer species that helps stabilize sandy soils.
compareHints: Mat sandbur differs from its coastal relative, coastal sandbur, by its lower, more spreading growth habit and slightly smaller burs. Chinese pennisetum, also in the same genus, produces soft, fluffy seed heads instead of spiny burs and grows much taller. If you're dealing with painful, tiny spines on a low-growing grass, you've found mat sandbur.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its Cenchrus relatives mat sandbur and coastal sandbur, which are low-growing weedy grasses with spiny, painful seed burs, Chinese pennisetum is a tall, ornamental clumping grass with soft, feathery plumes.
Coastal sandbur differs from its relative mat sandbur by preferring coastal sandy habitats rather than inland disturbed areas.
